newsitem.title: BRAZIL: "Interesting times" with new Brazil cenbank chief.
newsitem.headline: "Interesting times" with new Brazil cenbank chief.

text.p: With the nomination of Gustavo Franco as the next head of the Central Bank, Brazil's monetary purists have won a power struggle against the big spenders, and "interesting times" can be expected ahead.

Diplomats and political analysts said Wednesday that Franco's appointment, once confirmed by the Senate, sent out a strong message that there would be no change in Brazil's tight monetary policies or in the strong real currency.

"The signal that Brazil wants to send is 'we're not changing!'" said a Western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. "That's the gospel and for that there's nobody better than Franco in the eyes of the market."
But in the political realm, various people will be licking their wounds and waiting for 41-year-old Franco to stumble.

That will be particularly true in the run-up to the 1998 presidential polls when pressure on the government to spend more will rise to perhaps unbearable levels and Franco's tight-fisted approach to Brazil's fiscal woes will be fiercely challenged.

Political analysts said Franco's nomination was a slap in the face of Communications Minister Sergio Motta, a leading member of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB) and a known Franco foe.

It was also seen strengthening the hand of the rightist Liberal Front Party (PFL) because Franco was expected to place more emphasis on pushing for the approval of key fiscal reforms, slowly passing through Congress.
"The PSDB has lost another battle and the PFL has been strengthened," said political scientist David Fleischer.
"Big losers are also the exporters and those calling for more popular economic policies in 1998. There will be interesting times ahead."

Financial daily Gazeta Mercantil noted Franco's nomination to replace outgoing Central Bank president Gustavo Loyola could upset the balance of power between diehard monetarists like Franco and the more liberal, like monetary policy director Francisco Lopes. Loyola is seen as a neutral counterbalance to the radicals on the bank's board.
"Gustavo Loyola's exit leaves the Central Bank without the counterweight that has in the last 26 months kept the boardroom...in balance," the paper wrote.
"Only time will tell what consequences this will have on the necessary harmony in the economic team."
Once his name is approved by the Senate, seen happening by August 10, Franco will face several challenges.
A diplomat said he would have to find a safe way to bring Brazil's real currency, regarded by many as up to 20 percent overvalued against the dollar, down to reasonable levels.
The he will have to face down political pressure for more spending in election year.
Political analysts said one challenge Franco will face will be completing the work Loyola began in cleaning up the financial system and strengthening banking supervision.
He will also have to decide how to tackle money-laundering, an area where pressure from Washington has been mounting but where Brasilia has been dragging its feet, analysts said.
